violation: RESTATED 2026-08-01 - the original claim is only partly true on this toolchain, and the untrue half was load-bearing. The entry said core/agentmgr signals `by PID with no epoch guard`. It does not. os.Process.signal dispatches to pidfdSendSignal whenever p.handle is non-nil (go1.26.5 src/os/exec_unix.go:84), and os/exec sets that handle via pidfd_open on Linux 5.4+. So the five call sites - go_agent.go:465 (SIGTERM), :492 (Kill), :562 (SIGHUP), python_agent.go:507 (SIGTERM), :533 (Kill); note the original entry listed three and missed the two Kill sites - deliver through pidfd_send_signal against a handle bound at fork, and return ErrProcessDone after Wait without sending. That is a STRONGER guarantee than procsig's: a handle cannot refer to a recycled PID at all, whereas an epoch check compares two numbers. WHAT REMAINS TRUE, and is what this entry now names: gapi's local signal safety is INHERITED from the Go runtime and nothing in gapi asserts, documents or tests that dependency. It lapses silently if p.handle is nil - a kernel without pidfd, or a Process that has been Released - in which case os falls back to pidSignal, a raw kill by PID, which is exactly the original hazard. core/procsig exists, is tested, and has ZERO callers inside gapi (its only consumers are in goblin), so the mechanism this entry funded is unused here. ORIGINAL VIOLATION: Local signal delivery has no start_epoch check and no pidfd_open/pidfd_send_signal guard, leaving the kernel-level PID-recycling ABA hazard open.
rule: research/global-uuid-based-process-identity DDR-5 (start_epoch as cluster-level pidfd; end-to-end ABA safety)
exit: RESOLVED 2026-08-01 - closed on two gates, neither of which is a comment. Part (2) was already satisfied: the bare-PID delivery path is the CRIU-restored process, tracked as GAPI-DIV-046, and that entry is resolved - adopt captures procsig.StartEpoch at adopt time and delivery goes through procsig. Part (1) now has both forms the exit offered. TEST: core/agentmgr TestGoAgent_SpawnCarriesPidfd starts a real GoAgent through the ordinary Start path and asserts this process holds a pidfd whose /proc/self/fdinfo Pid is exactly that agent's pid. The handle is read from the kernel's view of our file descriptors rather than by reflecting into os.Process, so a field rename cannot break the gate and an absent handle cannot hide behind one. STARTUP: Phase0Deps gains RequirePidfd, run before every other obligation because it is a precondition and not an obligation, and RunPhase0 fails closed on it; core/procsig.RequirePidfd probes by opening a pidfd on self, so a false negative cannot come from the target rather than the kernel. REVERT-PROVEN BOTH WAYS. The agent test was broken by calling Release on the started process - which is not a synthetic sabotage but the second lapse this entry itself names - and went red naming the pid and the hazard. The boot gate was broken by keeping the call and discarding its result, the failure mode where a check reports a fault and lets boot continue, and TestPhase0_RefusesWithoutPidfd caught it because it asserts nothing after the precondition ran, not merely that an error came back. Restored byte-identical each time. TestRequirePidfd_RealKernel keeps the success path exercised so the gate cannot pass by never being reachable. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS ENTRY'S OWN TEXT, found while closing it. Its violation says core/procsig has ZERO callers inside gapi; that stopped being true when GAPI-DIV-045 and -046 landed - core/agentmgr/adopted.go and core/agentmgr/checkpoint.go both import it. And the five call sites have drifted from go_agent.go:465/492/562 and python_agent.go:507/533 to :479/506/576 and :519/545. Both are staleness in the record, not new divergence. RESIDUALS, stated rather than solved. Phase0Deps.RequirePidfd is nil-skippable like every other field there, so a wiring that omits it silently loses the startup half and nothing asserts the wiring - the same trap GAPI-DIV-046's exit names about checkFileLength. It is a bounded residual because the TEST half is not nil-skippable and holds the line in CI unconditionally. goblin's half of that residual is CLOSED as of 2026-08-01: gapi was tagged v0.1.0-proto2c, goblin re-vendored it and set RequirePidfd in internal/supervisor/pid1_wiring.go (goblin pull request 22), and the precondition has since executed inside real guests - goblind completes Phase 0 in the Privileged VM Checks job with the check active. The correction is recorded rather than the sentence being deleted, because this entry was closed partly for keeping stale facts about itself and silently fixing them would repeat that. What survives is symmetric and unchanged in kind: nothing asserts that EITHER repo's Phase0Deps literal keeps the field, so deleting the line goes green in gapi and in goblin alike. An AST gate asserting the literal carries it would close both at once; goblin already has that pattern in core/consensus/fsm_operator_keys_caller_test.go. And the test proves the handle exists at spawn, not that every later signal uses it; a Release between start and stop would be caught only by running that same assertion again. PRIOR EXIT (2026-08-01 reopening, superseded by the closure above): REOPENED AND NARROWED 2026-08-01. Do not close this by routing the five child call sites through procsig: that would replace a handle-based guarantee with a weaker epoch comparison and change nothing observable. Close instead on the dependency being ASSERTED rather than inherited. Two things must hold. (1) The pidfd path is required, not hoped for: either a startup or doctor check that fails when pidfd is unavailable, or a test that fails if a spawned agent's process does not carry a pidfd handle - so a kernel or toolchain that silently drops to pidSignal produces a red build rather than a quiet return to the original hazard. (2) Any delivery path where gapi holds a PID NUMBER rather than a handle goes through procsig, because there the epoch check is the only guard available. The known instance of (2) is the CRIU-restored process and is tracked separately as GAPI-DIV-046; this entry does not close until (1) is gated. Documenting the dependency in a comment is NOT an exit - a comment cannot fail a build. The two messages differed by one trailing newline, so no signature the shipped CLI produced could ever verify. The same function trimmed for the digest comparison and did NOT trim for the signature check, which is what hid it: 'if actual != strings.TrimSpace(string(hashData))' immediately above 'if !Verify(pub, hashData, sigBytes)'. Found by the 2026-07-29 documentation audit while checking whether the documented signing workflow actually worked.

exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29: verification now covers the CANONICAL digest - Verify(pub, []byte(actual), sigBytes) - matching what the signer covers. Signing the digest rather than the sidecar's bytes is the sounder contract: it keeps the chain pubkey -> digest -> binary independent of how the sidecar is spelled, so a .b3 rewritten without a trailing newline still verifies against an unchanged binary. The doc comment, which had described the old (broken) intent as signing 'the .b3 file's bytes', was corrected to match. ROOT CAUSE OF THE GAP IN COVERAGE: no test ever crossed the two paths. Any test that signed and verified through a single helper would have passed against the broken code, because both halves would have used the same message. The new core/crypto/verifybinary_test.go therefore reproduces the CLI's signing form and the build's sidecar format separately, then verifies through the discovery path. Artifacts: six new tests pass; and, decisively, reverting the one-line fix makes three of them FAIL with the exact symptom ('a signature made the way the CLI makes them did not verify', 'a signature over the sidecar bytes was accepted') - confirmed by experiment, then restored. One test pins the contract against future drift by asserting that a signature over the sidecar bytes is REJECTED. Full gate: 'mage lint' 0 issues / 0 nosec, 'mage test' green. HOW IT SHIPPED WITH A GREEN SUITE - the most transferable part: production-mode signature acceptance WAS covered, by core/agentmgr/safety_test.go TestSafeToExecute_ProductionAcceptsValidSignature. It passed because its helper signBinary signed []byte(hash+"\n") - the sidecar bytes - which is what the verifier happened to check, and its own comment described that as 'the gapictl agent verify convention'. The test mirrored the IMPLEMENTATION rather than the CONTRACT, so it stayed green while the shipped CLI produced signatures nothing could verify. Fixing the verifier made that test fail, which is how the mirroring was found. signBinary now signs what 'gapictl crypto sign' signs, and its comment records why. The lesson generalises: a helper that constructs its own input by copying the code under test cannot detect a contract mismatch, however many assertions follow it. All eight safety tests pass with the corrected helper, including the tampered-binary and wrong-key negatives, so the contract was tightened rather than loosened.

violation: All three systemd-style timer prefixes are aliases for the same behaviour. parseSystemdSchedule matches OnUnitActiveSec=, OnBootSec= and OnStartupSec=, strips whichever prefix matched, parses the remaining duration, and returns an IntervalSchedule in every case - the prefix itself is discarded. So OnBootSec=1m does not run once, one minute after boot; it runs every minute forever, which is what OnUnitActiveSec=1m means. OnStartupSec is the same. The doc comment on ParseSchedule and docs/features.md both described the systemd semantics, so an operator declaring SCHEDULE = "OnBootSec=1h" for a once-per-boot task got an hourly job instead - a silent behavioural difference, not an error. Discovery's own default for a timer with no SCHEDULE is OnUnitActiveSec=60s, which is the only spelling whose name currently matches what it does.

exit: RESOLVED 2026-07-29 by implementing the two missing semantics rather than rejecting the prefixes, so a systemd-compatible spelling carries systemd behaviour. A new OnceSchedule fires a single time at a fixed instant and then returns the ZERO time; the Schedule interface documents zero as 'exhausted' and TimerAgent.run stops on it instead of busy-waiting. OnStartupSec anchors to the parse instant, OnBootSec to the system boot, read from unix.Sysinfo rather than /proc/uptime so it works before the PID-1 early mount phase; non-Linux builds return time.Now, degrading OnBootSec to OnStartupSec, which is announced in the doc comment rather than silent. The prefix table now carries each prefix's anchor as data, so adding one without deciding its anchor is a compile-time hole rather than a silent alias - that omission is what produced the bug. A missed elapse point fires immediately, once (the run loop clamps a negative delay to zero), matching systemd's monotonic-timer behaviour rather than cancelling. ParseScheduleAt takes now and boot injected so the relative forms are testable without waiting on a real clock. ARTIFACTS: core/agentmgr/schedule_semantics_test.go asserts fire COUNT and fire INSTANT per prefix - OnUnitActiveSec repeats, the other two fire exactly once, and OnBootSec=45m resolves to 15m from a now that is 30m past boot, proving the anchor. A Go agent is a single file named <name>.go.<type> declaring consts and lifecycle functions - no main, no flag parsing, no hand-written describe JSON, no signal handling. THE RUNTIME LIVES IN adk/go/AGENT AND NEVER adk/go, as the entry demanded: gopy binds every exported symbol in adk/go into the Python ADK's native module, so a Run or Register there would leak this runtime into Python's C bindings. ALL THREE CONSEQUENCES CLOSED. (b) CONTROL EVENTS ARE EMITTED: the runtime sends starting, ready, stopping, stopped and error on stdout, which is the channel streamControl scans. So the shared core CANNOT simply be 'move adk/go/agent's functions up into adk/go' - that re-leaks the Go agent runtime into Python's C bindings, which is the defect the package layout exists to prevent. It needs either a third package both import, or an explicit narrow gopy-facing shim in adk/go that wraps it and exports only the describe surface. The deletion is the load-bearing half: while that literal exists, the two schemas are two schemas. DEMONSTRATED BY FAILURE, and it must be this direction rather than a green run: add a key to the shared Go definition and show BOTH languages' --describe carry it with NO Python edit. A green parity suite proves the two agree today, which is what it has always proved and is not the property this entry is about. RESIDUAL, and it is the reason this exit does not promise a total merge: READINESS DETECTION IS GENUINELY LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC. _await_ready's thread-liveness rules have no Go analogue - Go has no non-daemon thread concept to enumerate - so that piece is the one most likely to stay divergent, and pretending otherwise would trade a real duplication for a false abstraction. The honest target is that the DECLARATIVE surface has one definition and the RUNTIME halves may differ, with the difference written down. COST IS AN ESTIMATE, NOT A FINDING: this reads as a large refactor, and this ledger's own record is that such estimates run high more often than low (GOBLIN-DIV-047 and -050 both predicted more work than was needed). surface: core/mounts/mounts.go (MountSpec, Mounter, EarlyMounts, MountEarly); core/agentmgr/discovery.go (the Agent interface and the type routing); adk/go/agent/spec.go (Register's required Start); goblin internal/supervisor/targets.go (the target vocabulary a mount would join)
violation: There is no mount agent type, so the only filesystems gapi can mount are the six hardcoded in EarlyMounts. A deployment needing a data disk, a bind mount or an NFS share has nowhere to declare it, and no way to order an agent after it. systemd models this as a first-class unit type; gapi models it as a Go slice. THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS AND IS THE REASON THIS IS TRACTABLE: core/mounts has MountSpec{Source, Target, FSType, Flags, Options}, a Mounter interface with Mount/IsMounted/MkdirAll, and MountEarly which is idempotent over premounted targets and fails closed. What is missing is the agent kind, not the syscall surface. WHY IT IS A NEW KIND RATHER THAN A NEW TYPE STRING: every current Agent implementation supervises a PROCESS and derives liveness from process state. A mount has no pid, no stdout, no readiness handshake and no control events. Start is a syscall that returns immediately and 'active' is a STATE PREDICATE - is the target in mountinfo - which core/mounts already answers via IsMounted. AGREED SHAPE, operator 2026-08-02: a mount agent is CODE like any other, written in Go or Python, so the <name>.<lang>.<type> filename invariant holds unchanged. It is the socket pattern exactly: the agent DECLARES what the supervisor needs (Source, Target, FSType, Options, as a socket agent declares ListenStream), the SUPERVISOR performs the privileged operation (mount(2), as it binds and passes fd 3), and the agent's code runs against the result. That also removes the security objection to a declarative type: the supervisor mounts from metadata it can validate rather than from arbitrary agent code.
rule: cooperative-ecosystem-manifesto section 5 (the SDK's parity contract: a capability must be expressible in both languages with identical semantics); design/gapi-architecture.md (socket activation as the model for a privileged operation the supervisor owns and the agent consumes)
exit: A mount agent type discovered, ordered, started and stopped like any other, with these four decisions already taken and NOT to be relitigated. (1) START IS NOT REQUIRED for Type="mount". Register panics without Start today; that is relaxed for mounts rather than satisfied with a synthesized default, because if Start is always present its presence stops meaning anything. Absent Start makes 'this agent has post-mount work' visible in the source at a glance. (2) PARENT ORDERING IS DERIVED FROM Target, NEVER DECLARED. /var/lib/data implies /var/lib. This is what systemd does - nested mount points acquire BOTH a requirement and an ordering dependency automatically - and derived is strictly better than declared because a declared parent can be wrong while a derived one cannot. (3) ID MUST EQUAL THE ESCAPED Target: ID="var-lib-data" for Target="/var/lib/data". This is how duplicate mount points become unrepresentable rather than merely detected, and it costs no new mechanism: discovery is ALREADY first-ID-wins by agent ID, so two agents claiming one mount point collide as one ID and mask each other with the same override semantics as everything else. systemd gets this by requiring the unit filename to match Where=; gapi keeps <name>.<lang>.<type> and gets it from a field validation instead. (4) SYSTEM SCOPE ONLY. A mount agent in user scope is a privilege-escalation primitive unless confined to a user namespace, so a mount discovered in user scope is REFUSED with a reason rather than quietly skipped. This is the first real job for the Scope parameter beyond selecting directories. CLOSES ON: a test that declares a mount agent over a loopback or tmpfs target, asserts the supervisor mounted it (IsMounted true) before the agent's dependents start, and asserts reverse unmount at shutdown - run for BOTH languages, because a capability expressible in one is a parity break. DEMONSTRATED BY FAILURE: declare two agents with the same Target and show the second is masked rather than racing; and declare a mount in user scope and show it refused. EARLYMOUNTS IS DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE and deferred by the operator. The finding that shapes it, recorded now so it is not rediscovered: HIERARCHY ORDERING IS INSUFFICIENT FOR THE EARLY SET. The table is /dev, /proc, /sys, /sys/fs/cgroup, /run, /tmp, and only cgroup2-after-/sys is a parent/child edge - /dev before /proc is declared sequence. So the early set cannot use the ordering rule a mount agent would, and it is a shared type with two drivers rather than a merge. The bootstrap constraint stands regardless: agent discovery reads a filesystem and execs binaries, so nothing can be discovered before /proc and /run exist. WRITE FIRST, whichever way that goes: a string-to-Flags parser test that parses the option string form of each of the six EarlyMounts and asserts it equals the hardcoded uintptr bitmask. Both answers need that parser, and the test either validates or falsifies the shared-vocabulary premise before any design rests on it. LATER, NOT NOW: systemd's RequiresMountsFor= - any unit naming a PATH and the supervisor resolving it to the mount agents covering that path, parents included. It is the generalisation worth stealing once the type exists.
